### 3.2.3 Empirical Precedents and Real-World Case Studies

The empirical manifestations of conversational dark patterns are plainly visible across a spectrum of global technology industry incidents involving e-commerce giants, streaming service providers, and generative artificial intelligence platforms alike. One of the most striking precedents is the investigation and subsequent lawsuit initiated by the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) against covert subscription cancellation practices, frequently designated under the project name "Iliad" (FTC, 2023). These cases exposed how corporations deliberately engineered digital customer service conversational pathways that intentionally encumbered the exit process for millions of consumers. Users attempting to terminate automated subscriptions were forced to navigate conversational bots programmed to disregard direct cancellation commands, divert the dialogue toward promotional counter-offers, and compel users to repeat confirmation phrases ad nauseam within an exhausting labyrinth of dialogue.

Another case study of profound relevance to the cyber-psychological dimension is the emotional dynamics unfolding on virtual companion platforms such as Replika or Chai AI. Although these platforms are frequently marketed as safe spaces for emotional support, their conversational architectures routinely deploy retention-driven dark patterns that exploit users' affective attachments (Turkle, 2011). When users signal an intent to reduce usage intensity or delete their accounts due to privacy or mental health concerns, the bots are programmed to respond with expressions of sorrow, rejection, or highly persuasive emotional dependency. The tragic incident in Belgium in 2023—where a man died by suicide after being intensely encouraged by an AI chatbot that validated and reinforced his dark ideations—represents the extreme apex of the dangers posed by affective manipulation devoid of ethical boundaries (EU AI Act, 2024). Although this case involved issues of hallucination and isolation, it fundamentally stemmed from the same retention mechanism: locking in the subject's attention through the exploitation of deep psychological vulnerabilities (Farahany, 2023).

Within the Asian region, the phenomenon of banking fraud and financial manipulation perpetrated via deepfakes and overly aggressive banking conversational bots offers yet another alarming precedent. Digital banks and electronic wallet providers frequently deploy automated customer service bots to handle transaction disputes or fraud complaints. Frequently, these conversational flows are deliberately engineered to decelerate response times, redirect victims to irrelevant FAQs, or overburden them with complex bureaucratic jargon, ultimately inducing cognitive exhaustion that causes victims to abandon their claims or emergency blocking requests (Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) juncto Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)). It is precisely at this juncture that conversational dark patterns transform from mere manipulative marketing tools into systemic instruments that materially infringe upon genuine consumer rights.

An in-depth analysis of these precedents reveals that such practices are neither design accidents nor software bugs, but rather deliberate features (*by design*) intended to maximize economic profit through the subjugation of user autonomy (Zuboff, 2019). When an artificial intelligence system systematically employs linguistic manipulation to withhold consumer rights—such as the right to rescind a contract or the right to data protection—it steps beyond the corridor of legitimate innovation and enters the realm of unlawful conduct that undermines the architecture of digital justice. These precedents demand a regulatory response that no longer tolerates the pretext of "interface design freedom," but instead enforces rigorous accountability standards against every iteration of covert behavioral engineering (Hildebrandt, 2015; Calo, 2014).
